rules.title: The Partitive Case
rules.explanation: Finnish marks an object that is **partial, uncountable or unbounded** — and any object after a **negation** — with the **partitive** case. The ending is **-a / -ä**, **-ta / -tä** or **-tta / -ttä**, and the choice between **a** and **ä** follows **vowel harmony**: back-vowel words take **-a** (talo → talo**a**), front-vowel words take **-ä** (kylä → kylä**ä**). Compare the whole and the part: **Juon vettä** (I drink [some] water) sees the object as unbounded, so 'vesi' becomes 'vettä'.

noticing_prompts.q: In 'Juon vettä', which word is the object in the partitive?
'talo' has back vowels. Does its partitive take -a or -ä?

structured_input.question: Why is 'vettä' in the partitive?
options: The object is an unbounded, uncountable amount (some water)
It is the subject of the sentence
structured_input.feedback: An unbounded or partial object (some water) takes the partitive, so 'vesi' becomes 'vettä'.

structured_input.question: Which do you usually drink? Choose the true one.
structured_input.feedback: Each object is in the partitive (an unbounded amount): vettä, kahvia, teetä.

quiz.feedback_why: The object of 'puhua' is unbounded, so 'englanti' takes the partitive '-a' (back-vowel harmony).
'vesi' is an uncountable object here, so it takes the partitive 'vettä' (front-vowel harmony).

communicative_production.prompt: Write a sentence about something you drink or eat, using a partitive object.
communicative_production.hint: An unbounded or uncountable object takes the partitive (-a / -ä).
